title: Epistle of Rav Sherira Gaon
text: And as long as the Holy Temple (בית המקדש) stood, each and every one of the great Sages would teach his students the reasons of the Torah, the Mishnah, and the Talmud, using words he composed himself at that time, and he would instruct his students as he saw fit. Wisdom was abundant, and they did not need other exertions. The only dispute among them was regarding the laying of hands (Semichah). And when Shammai (שמאי) and Hillel (הלל) arose, they only disagreed on three matters, as Rav Huna (רב הונא) said: "In three places Shammai and Hillel disagreed." But when the Temple was destroyed, and they went to Beitar (ביתר), and Beitar was also destroyed, the Sages were scattered in every direction. Due to those tumults, persecutions, and confusions that occurred at that time, the students did not serve their masters sufficiently, and disputes multiplied. From the time Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai (רבן יוחנן בן זכאי) passed away, and Rabban Gamliel (רבן גמליאל) arose—and Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas (רבי דוסא בן הרכינס) and others of those early Sages were still alive—there was the dispute between the House of Shammai (בית שמאי) and the House of Hillel (בית הלל). And even though the House of Shammai was rejected and the halacha was established according to the House of Hillel, there was still a dispute in the generation of Rabban Gamliel in other matters between Rabbi Eliezer (רבי אליעזר), who was a Shammaite, and Rabbi Yehoshua (רבי יהושע), who were students of Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai.

And there were also in that generation Rabbi Yose the Galilean (רבי יוסי הגלילי), Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah (רבי אלעזר בן עזריה), Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri (רבי יוחנן בן נורי), Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka (רבי יוחנן בן ברוקא), Rabbi Hanina ben Teradion (רבי חנינא בן תרדיון), Rabbi Elazar ben Teradion (רבי אלעזר בן תרדיון), Rabbi Elazar Hisma (רבי אלעזר חסמא), Abba Halafta (אבא חלפתא), and Rabbi Yose ben Kisma (רבי יוסי בן קיסמא). And before them were Shimon ben Azzai (שמעון בן עזאי) and Shimon ben Zoma (שמעון בן זומא), and many other Sages who lived in that generation.

And secondary to them were those who were their students and colleagues. They lived in their days, such as Rabbi Akiva (רבי עקיבא), Rabbi Elazar of Modi'in (רבי אלעזר המודעי), Rabbi Yehudah ben Bava (רבי יהודה בן בבא), and Rabbi Yishmael (רבי ישמעאל). Up until that time, Rabbi Yehudah (רבי יהודה) was in Nisibis (נציבין), and although he was there during the time of the Temple, he remained there even after its destruction. This was a significant period, as it was after they had settled down from the destruction of the Temple. At that time, they sat down to grasp their halachot that had been lost in the confusion of the destruction, the persecution, and the disputes between the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel.

And the Sages were numerous at that time. Among them were great rabbis who had benches in the study hall and sat upon them, and among them were other Sages who sat before them. On the day Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah (רבי אלעזר בן עזריה) was appointed, we say that many benches were added to the study hall. Rabbi Yohanan (רבי יוחנן) said: Abba Yose ben Dostai (אבא יוסי בן דוסתאי) and the Rabbis dispute this; one said four hundred benches, and one said seven hundred. And if this many were added, how many must the original number have been!

And Rabbi Akiva (רבי עקיבא) surrendered himself to martyrdom after Rabbi Yose ben Kisma (רבי יוסי בן קיסמא) passed away. And Rabbi Hanina ben Teradion (רבי חנינא בן תרדיון) was killed, and wisdom was diminished after them. Rabbi Akiva raised many students, but there was a persecution upon the students of Rabbi Akiva, and the reliance of Israel was upon the second group of Rabbi Akiva's students. For the Sages said: Rabbi Akiva had twelve thousand pairs of students from Gevat to Antipatris, and all of them died between Passover and Shavuot, and the world remained desolate until he came to our Rabbis in the South and taught them: Rabbi Meir (רבי מאיר), Rabbi Yose (רבי יוסי), Rabbi Yehudah (רבי יהודה), Rabbi Shimon (רבי שמעון), and Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua (רבי אלעזר בן שמוע). And they are the ones who established the Torah at that time, as stated in Yevamot.

And Rabbi Meir (רבי מאיר) was learned, sharp, and more brilliant than all of them, and Rabbi Akiva (רבי עקיבא) ordained him, even though he was young. And the others were ordained after Rabbi Akiva by Rabbi Yehudah ben Bava (רבי יהודה בן בבא), and he then re-ordained Rabbi Meir. As we say: Rav Yehudah (רב יהודה) said that Rav (רב) said, "Indeed, may that man be remembered for good, and his name is Rabbi Yehudah ben Bava, for were it not for him, the laws of fines would have been forgotten from Israel." For once the wicked kingdom decreed a persecution against Israel: whoever ordains will be killed, whoever is ordained will be killed, a city in which they ordain will be destroyed, and the boundaries within which they ordain will be uprooted. What did Rabbi Yehudah ben Bava do? He went and sat between two great mountains, between two large cities, between Usha and Shefaram, and he ordained five elders there: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehudah, Rabbi Yose, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua. And Rav Avia (רב אויא) adds: also Rabbi Nehemiah (רבי נחמיה). And we raise a difficulty: But Rabbah bar bar Hana (רבה בר בר חנה) said that Rabbi Yohanan (רבי יוחנן) said: "Whoever says Rabbi Akiva did not ordain Rabbi Meir is nothing but mistaken." And we answer: Rabbi Akiva ordained him, but they did not accept him because he was young, and then Rabbi Yehudah ben Bava ordained him, and they accepted him.

And in this generation, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel (רבן שמעון בן גמליאל) was the Nasi, and Rabbi Natan (רבי נתן) came up from Babylon and was the Head of the Court, as explained at the end of the Gemara Horayot. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said to Rabbi Natan: "Granted that your father's belt helped you become Head of the Court, but did it help you become Nasi?" And Rabbi Meir (רבי מאיר) was the Sage of the generation, as explained there as well, that when Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Meir would enter the study hall, the entire assembly would stand before them.

And there were also great Sages in that generation who constantly disseminated Torah, such as Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka (רבי ישמעאל בן רבי יוחנן בן ברוקא), Rabbi Yehoshua ben Karha (רבי יהושע בן קרחא), Rabbi Elazar ben Yehudah (רבי אלעזר בן יהודה), Rabbi Shimon ben Yehudah (רבי שמעון בן יהודה), Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon (רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון), Rabbi Yaakov of Kefar Hittaya (רבי יעקב איש כפר חיטייא), Rabbi Frida (רבי פרידא), Rabbi Peda the First (רבי פדה קדמאה), Rabbi Zecharya ben HaKatzav (רבי זכריה בן הקצב), Rabbi Matya ben Harash (רבי מתיא בן חרש), Rabbi Elazar ben Yirmeyah (רבי אלעזר בן ירמיה), Hanin ben Pinchas (חנין בן פנחס), Abba Hanin (אבא חנין), P'limo (פלימו), Symmachus (סומכוס), Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar (רבי שמעון בן אלעזר), Rabbi Hanina ben Gamliel (רבי חנינא בן גמליאל), Rabbi Yehudah ben Gamla (רבי יהודה בן גמלא), Rabbi Elazar ben Taddai (רבי אלעזר בן תדאי), Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair (רבי פנחס בן יאיר), Rabbi Yaakov ben Dosai (רבי יעקב בן דוסאי), Issi ben Yehudah (איסי בן יהודה), Rabbi Hanina ben Hakinai (רבי חנינא בן חכינאי), Rabbi Yeshevav the Scribe (רבי ישבב הסופר), Rabbi Elazar HaKappar (רבי אלעזר הקפר), Rabbi Reuven the Astrobolite (רבי ראובן האיצטרובולי), and the Sages who were with them.

And all the days of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel (רבן שמעון בן גמליאל), he raised our Holy Rabbi [Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi] (רבנו הקדוש) his son to study Torah. As we say: When Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Karha (רבי יהושע בן קרחא) were sitting on benches, Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon (רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון) were sitting before them on the ground, asking and answering questions. They said, "We drink their water, yet they sit on the ground!" They built benches for them and brought them up. And Rabbi served those Sages, as Rabbi said: "When we were studying Torah with Rabbi Shimon (רבי שמעון) in Tekoa..." etc. And he learned the halachot of the Mishnah from them, as Rabbi said: "When I went to study Torah with Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua (רבי אלעזר בן שמוע), his students gathered against me like the roosters of Beit Bukya, and they did not allow me to learn anything except for one thing in our Mishnah: an androgynous person—one is liable to stoning over him as a male."

And when he reigned after his father, the sons of those Sages were with him, such as Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yose (רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי), Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehudah (רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה), Rabbi Yaakov of Kefar Hittaya (רבי יעקב איש כפר חיטייא), and other students such as Rabbi Hiyya (רבי חייא) who came up from Babylon, Rabbi Hanina b'Rabbi Hama (רבי חנינא ברבי חמא), Rabbi Efes (רבי אפס), Rabbi Gamliel (רבי גמליאל) and Rabbi Shimon (רבי שמעון), the sons of our Holy Rabbi, and Rabbi Yannai (רבי ינאי). And they disseminated much Torah.

And in all these years, all the halachot that had been pending in all the study halls were clarified, following the great loss during the destruction of the Temple and the doubts they had during those tumults. And all the disputes that arose in these three generations were decided, and the words of the individuals and the words of the majority became known among them, after the Sages exerted immense effort and scrutinized them exactingly, carefully examining the traditions and the Mishnayot to correct them. They did not add a single statement to the early ones from the Men of the Great Assembly; rather, they exerted immense effort and scrutinized deeply until they concluded what those early ones were saying and what they were practicing, until all their doubts were resolved.

And not a single one of the early ones wrote anything down until the end of the days of our Holy Rabbi (רבי). Likewise, they did not all recite with one mouth and one language, but they knew their reasons. And they were all of one mind, there was no dispute in their texts, and they knew what was universally agreed upon, what was disputed, what belonged to an individual, and what belonged to the majority. They did not have arranged texts and a known Mishnah that everyone recited with one mouth and one language; rather, those reasons and traditions that they knew, even though all the Sages were equal in them, each one would teach his students in whatever compilation he wished, in whatever manner he wished. Some took a short path, as we say: "The Mishnah of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov (רבי אליעזר בן יעקב) is small but pristine." And furthermore, we say: "A person should always teach his students by a short path." Some taught general rules, some taught specifics, and some expanded and explained comparisons. Each and every Sage taught as his master taught him. This one placed a matter first, and that one placed it later; this one shortened his language, and that one expanded it. And there were also those whose master was an individual who said a matter, and he taught it anonymously, even though it was known to him that it was an individual opinion, and we say: "A person is obligated to speak in the language of his master." And there are those who taught what seemed logical to them: one like this Tanna, and one like that Tanna. And because of this, they explain in the Gemara: "Whose view is this? It is Rabbi so-and-so." And we say: "Who is the Tanna for that which our Rabbis taught? It is according to this Tanna." And we say in several places: "He who taught this did not teach that." And we analyze the texts point by point, establishing the first part according to one Tanna and the final part according to another Tanna. And all these teachings were called Baraitot after Rabbi arranged our Mishnah.

And they used to say that initially there were thirteen aspects of disputes among the Sages in the Mishnah. And Rabbi (רבי) had learned all of them, as we learn in Tractate Nedarim: Rabbi had learned thirteen aspects of halacha; he taught seven of them to Rabbi Hiyya (רבי חייא). Rabbi became ill and forgot them; Rabbi Hiyya restored the seven before him, but those other six were lost. There was a certain launderer who used to listen to Rabbi when he reviewed them. Rabbi Hiyya went and learned them from the launderer, and then Rabbi Hiyya came and restored them before Rabbi. And when Rabbi saw that launderer, he said to him: "You have made me and Hiyya." And some say he said to him: "You made Hiyya, and Hiyya made me."

And when Rabbi (רבי) saw that there was so much variation in the teachings of the Sages—even though their reasoning culminated in the same point—he was concerned lest matters multiply and cause a loss. Since he saw that the heart was diminishing, the wellspring of wisdom was being sealed, and the Torah was departing. Just as we say: "If the early ones were angels, we are humans; if the early ones were humans, we are donkeys." And as Rabbi Yohanan (רבי יוחנן) said: "The heart of the early ones was like the entrance of the Ulam, and the later ones like the entrance of the Heichal." And we say: Who are the early ones? Rabbi Akiva (רבי עקיבא). The later ones? Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua (רבי אלעזר בן שמוע). And they said: "The fingernail of the early ones is better than the belly of the later ones." And it was bestowed upon Rabbi from Heaven that he had Torah and greatness, and everyone submitted to him all those years. As we say: Rabbah b'Reishei d'Rava (רבה בריה דרבא) said, and some say Rabbi Hillel b'Reishei d'Rabbi Wallas (רבי הילל בריה דרבי ואלס): "From the days of Moses until Rabbi, we have not found Torah and greatness in one place."

And the Sages rested in the days of Rabbi (רבי) from all persecution because of the friendship that existed between Antoninus (אנטונינוס) and Rabbi. And he agreed to arrange the halachot so that the Sages would recite them with one mouth and one language, and not that each one would recite a different text for himself. This was because those early ones before the destruction of the Temple did not need this, since it is an Oral Torah, and their reasons were not stated in fixed words like the Written Torah, but they knew and learned the reasons in their hearts. Each one taught his students like a person conversing with his friend, teaching them in whatever language he wished. And since they gathered in the Chamber of Hewn Stone and in arranged study halls to recite them immediately, and they had authority without distress and without fear, and Heaven assisted them, the reasons of the Torah were clear to them as a halacha given to Moses from Sinai, and they had no variance or dispute. As we say: Rabbi Yose (רבי יוסי) taught, "Initially, there was no dispute in Israel, but the court of seventy-one sat in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, and two courts of twenty-three... sat in the cities of Israel. If the matter needed to be asked..." and the whole Baraita, until the students of Shammai (שמאי) and Hillel (הלל) multiplied, who did not serve their masters sufficiently; disputes multiplied in Israel, and the Torah became like two Torahs. And the Sages afterward, in the days of Rabban Gamliel (רבן גמליאל) and Rabban Shimon (רבן שמעון) his son, were still debating and maintaining the disputes of the Tannaim among themselves, and it was impossible for them to recite them with one mouth and one language.

And in the days of Rabbi (רבי) [the son of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel], his endeavor was successful, and he arranged them and wrote them down, and the words of our Mishnah are as if Moses stated them from the mouth of the Almighty, and they are like a sign and a wonder. He did not compose them from his own heart, but rather they are those matters that the early ones before him used to study. And how do we know this? From that which we learned: "An incident occurred where Ben Zakkai (בן זכאי) examined the stalks of figs." And we say in the Gemara: "It makes sense that this is a general Ben Zakkai, for if it enters your mind that it is Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai (רבן יוחנן בן זכאי), here he calls him Ben Zakkai, and here he calls him Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai?" And we raise a difficulty: "But it is taught in a Baraita: An incident occurred where Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai examined the stalks of figs!" And we conclude: "Rather, he was a student sitting before his master [Hillel] and he said a matter, and his reasoning made sense to his master, and they established it in his name." Thus, from that time of Hillel (הלל) and Shammai (שמאי) when the Rabbis taught "An incident occurred where Ben Zakkai examined...", Rabbi taught it exactly this way in the Mishnah and did not change it.

And further, from that which we learned: "How do we extend the boundaries of the cities?" And Rabbi (רבי) said, "Is there anyone who can ask the people of Judah, who are exact in their language, whether we learn 'Mabrin' (מאברין) or 'Me'abrin' (מעברין)?" Thus, Rabbi himself, who arranged the Mishnah, was unsure how we learn it, and he said: "He who learns 'Mabrin' is not mistaken, and he who learns 'Me'abrin' is not mistaken. He who learns 'Mabrin' means like a limb (Ever); he who learns 'Me'abrin' means like a pregnant woman (Ubara)." We learn from this that in this language it was stated before Rabbi; some taught it this way, and some taught it that way.

And even the tractates were in doubt before Rabbi (רבי), since Rabbi Meir (רבי מאיר) said to Rabbi Natan (רבי נתן): "Let us say to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel (רבן שמעון בן גמליאל), 'Open and teach in Uktzin,' which he does not know." And the incident of Rabbi Yaakov ben Korshai (רבי יעקב בן קרשאי) who went and sat by the window of the upper room where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was sitting, and he studied and recited Uktzin. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said, "What is happening before us?" He applied his mind and learned it.

And there is a place where Rabbi (רבי) added explanations, such as that which we learned: "Boys may go out with knots, and princes with bells." This is how the Mishnah was from the mouth of the early ones, and Rabbi added to it and explained: "And any person, but the Sages spoke of the usual practice," aside from matters that were taught in his days and in the days after him, as we say: "This is the first Mishnah; the later Mishnah said..." etc. And like Tractate Eduyot, which was taught on the day Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah (רבי אלעזר בן עזריה) was appointed, as we say: "Even Eduyot was taught on that day, and any place we learn 'on that day' refers to the day they sat Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah in the Yeshiva."

And Rabbi (רבי) taught for us within it, afterward, matters that were taught in the days of his father, such as: "Rabbi Yose (רבי יוסי) says six things from the leniencies of the House of Shammai and the stringencies of the House of Hillel"; and such as: "Rabbi Yehudah (רבי יהודה) said, Heaven forbid that Akavya (עקביא) was excommunicated, for the Temple courtyard is not locked upon any person in Israel equal in wisdom and fear of sin as Akavya ben Mahalalel (עקביא בן מהללאל)..." etc. But regarding other tractates, even though the earlier Sages taught their reasons, Rabbi arranged them as halacha. And some of them he would teach in their original language, and some of them he would teach as he saw fit.

And an anonymous Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir (רבי מאיר), and not because Rabbi Meir said it from his own heart, but it was that path of learning that Rabbi Meir had acquired. And in the way that Rabbi Meir taught his students, Rabbi (רבי) grasped that tradition and established it to be taught to everyone. And Rabbi Meir grasped his path of tradition from Rabbi Akiva (רבי עקיבא) his master, and Rabbi Akiva received it from his early masters, as we say: Rabbi Yohanan (רבי יוחנן) said, "An anonymous Mishnah is Rabbi Meir, an anonymous Tosefta is Rabbi Nehemiah (רבי נחמיה), an anonymous Sifra is Rabbi Yehudah (רבי יהודה), an anonymous Sifrei is Rabbi Shimon (רבי שמעון), and all of them are according to Rabbi Akiva."

And these Baraitot of the Tosefta, Sifra, and Sifrei—all these Baraitot were taught by the earlier Sages, and Rabbi Yehudah (רבי יהודה), Rabbi Nehemiah (רבי נחמיה), and Rabbi Shimon (רבי שמעון) came and each collected his own. Sifra is Rabbi Yehudah, Tosefta is Rabbi Nehemiah, Sifrei is Rabbi Shimon, and our Mishnah is Rabbi Meir (רבי מאיר)—and all of them are according to Rabbi Akiva (רבי עקיבא), for they were all students of Rabbi Akiva.

But other Baraitot we do not concern ourselves with, because these were the elite Sages who collected and composed them, and they were the distinguished students of Rabbi Akiva (רבי עקיבא). And thus Rabbi Shimon (רבי שמעון) said to his students: "My sons, learn my measures, for my measures are terumah (elevated offerings) from the terumah of the measures of Rabbi Akiva." And we say: "The heart of the early ones is like the entrance of the Ulam, the later ones like the entrance of the Heichal," and we explain: the early ones—this is Rabbi Akiva. And the Sages explain that even the First Man (אדם הראשון) rejoiced in the Torah of Rabbi Akiva when the Holy One, Blessed be He, showed him every generation and its Sages. And also Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas (רבי דוסא בן הרכינס) said to Rabbi Akiva: "Are you Akiva ben Yosef whose name goes from one end of the world to the other?"

And the greatest of all the students of Rabbi Akiva (רבי עקיבא) was Rabbi Meir (רבי מאיר), as we say: Rabbi Aha b'Rabbi Hanina (רבי אחא בר חנינא) said: "It is revealed and known before the One who spoke and the world came into being that there was none like Rabbi Meir in his generation. And why did the Sages not establish the halacha like him? Because his colleagues could not fathom the depths of his mind, for he would say concerning the impure that it is pure and show proof for it, and concerning the pure that it is impure and show proof for it." And because of this, he was beloved to Rabbi Akiva, who ordained him in his youth.

And Rabbi (רבי) adopted the path of Rabbi Meir (רבי מאיר) in halacha, which was the path of Rabbi Akiva (רבי עקיבא), since Rabbi saw that Rabbi Meir's path was concise, easy to learn, and its matters were beautifully synthesized—each and every matter with what resembled it. His words were far more exact than all the other Tannaim; they contained no superfluous language, and each and every word conveyed a reason without unnecessary embellishments. It lacked nothing and added nothing extra, save in necessary places, maintaining a concise path.

And generally, every single word contains great and wondrous things, and not every wise person knows how to compose words in such a way, as it is written: "To man belong the preparations of the heart, but the answer of the tongue is from the Lord." And even though all the Sages were equal in reasons and laws, since Rabbi Akiva (רבי עקיבא) had a broad heart, and Rabbi Meir (רבי מאיר) his student also had a broad heart, their arrangement was beautiful and superior to all other Tannaim. Therefore, Rabbi collected it, added what existed in his own days, arranged it as he saw fit, and also explained within it all the essential points and the cores of the disputes of the Sages. For since he was a Sage who heard from the great masters who disputed, or from individuals who disputed and stated their views anonymously, if someone heard them, they might be misled. But when he explains it this way, doubt is removed, as we learned: Rabbi Yehudah (רבי יהודה) said, "Why were the words of an individual mentioned among the majority to nullify them? Because if a person says 'Thus...,' they can say to him, 'From where did you get this?' And if he says to them, 'I received it thus,' they say to him, 'Perhaps you heard it according to the words of so-and-so.'"

And when everyone saw the beauty of the arrangement of our Mishnah, the truth of its words, and the exactness of the matters, they all abandoned those texts they used to study and spread these halachot throughout all of Israel, and all the other halachot were left aside and became like Baraitot. Whoever delves into them is like one who delves into commentaries or expanded texts, but the reliance of Israel was upon these halachot. Israel accepted them when they saw them faithfully, and there was no one who disagreed with them.

In this manner, Rabbi (רבי) arranged the six orders of the Mishnah. It was not that the early ones left the majority of the work for the later ones; rather, the early ones did not need to compile texts. The matters they studied were oral, and each and every one of the Sages knew them by tradition and did not need to compile or write them down. This was true until the Temple was destroyed, and the students of those early Sages arose, who did not know as much as they did and needed to compile texts. For Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus (רבי אליעזר בן הורקנוס), who was the chief of the students of Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai (רבן יוחנן בן זכאי), when they asked him those matters explained in the chapter 'Shnei Se'irim'—such as "A certain woman baked dough," "A certain man conquered," "A mamzer," "A house," "A guilt offering"—he did not answer them anything but pushed them off. And it is taught: It was not because he wanted to deflect them with words, but because he never said a thing he had not heard from the mouth of his master.
And for this reason, Rabbi (רבי) needed to compile and arrange the six orders of the Mishnah, after the world had rested for two generations from that persecution of the destruction of the Temple.

And regarding the tractates where you saw early and late placement, when Rabbi (רבי) arranged our Mishnah, he did not order one tractate immediately after another, but rather taught each one individually. Whoever wished to place one earlier, did so, and whoever wished to place it later, did so, and we do not know which one Rabbi taught first. But the halachot and the chapters of each and every tractate, Rabbi arranged them one after another, as we say: Rav Huna (רב הונא) said, "Within one tractate we do not say 'there is no chronological order to the Mishnah,' but between two tractates we do say 'there is no chronological order to the Mishnah.'" And any one of them, one could say perhaps Rabbi taught it first. And where we find an anonymous ruling and then a dispute in one tractate, we say the halacha does not follow the anonymous ruling (or a dispute and then an anonymous ruling in one tractate, we say the halacha follows the anonymous Mishnah), but between two tractates we do not say this because they have no set order. And Rav Yosef (רב יוסף) also held this view. However, we say regarding Bava Kamma, Bava Metzia, and Bava Batra that they are all one tractate.

And regarding what you asked: "What is the reason they placed Yoma (יומא) before Shekalim (שקלים)?" We in the Yeshiva learn Shekalim and then Yoma. But certainly, we learn Sukkah (סוכה) before Yom Tov (יום טוב), and after that certainly Rosh Hashanah (ראש השנה). And it is possible that Rabbi (רבי) taught them in a different order. However, one can say that Tractate Shabbat (שבת) must be placed first because Shabbat is very important. And after it Tractate Eruvin (עירובין) because it is similar to it and deals with the same subject. And after it Tractate Pesachim (פסחים), because it is the first of all the appointed times and festivals of the whole year. And after it Shekalim, which precedes it and is like one of its subjects. And after Shekalim we learn Yoma, which is similar to Shabbat and Eruvin because Yom Kippur is like Shabbat. And after the order of Yoma we learn Tractate Sukkah, because it is after Yom Kippur and is a great festival. And after Tractate Sukkah we learn Tractate Yom Tov, because it is the same subject. And after Yom Tov we learn Tractate Rosh Hashanah, so that Tractate Ta'anit (תענית) can be taught after it, because after Rosh Hashanah is the time of planting and the time of rain, and it is considered one subject.

This is how the Sages are accustomed to teaching, and if one wishes to advance or delay them, he has permission. Even though we see in some tractates that there is an order, as we say, "Let us see, the Tanna just finished Tractate X..." For example, in Tractate Sotah we say in the Gemara, "Let us see, the Tanna just finished Tractate Nazir." And in Tractate Shevuot we say, "Let us see, the Tanna just finished Makkot," implying that they do have an order.

And regarding the Tosefta of Rabbi Hiyya (רבי חייא), he certainly arranged it, and it is not resolved for us whether it was arranged in the days of Rabbi (רבי) or after him. But without a doubt, the halachot of our Mishnah were arranged before the Tosefta, and the words of the Tosefta clearly follow our Mishnah and are based upon it. And it is not resolved for us whether Rabbi Hiyya passed away in the days of Rabbi or after him, as we wonder in the chapter "HaNose" why Rabbi instructed that Rabbi Hanina bar Hama (רבי חנינא בר חמא) should sit at the head, and we say, "But isn't there Rabbi Hiyya who is greater than him?" And we answer, "Rabbi Hiyya had passed away." And even though we object, "But Rabbi Hiyya said, 'I saw the grave of Rabbi and shed tears upon it!'" and furthermore, "When Rabbi died, the priesthood was abolished," and furthermore, "When Rabbi fell ill, Rabbi Hiyya went in to visit him..." etc. And we say, "If you want, say reverse it, and if you want, say do not reverse it, since Rabbi Hiyya was engaged in a mitzvah, he thought he would not be harmed." Thus, we remain in doubt.

However, the Sages say that the Tosefta was arranged in the days of Rabbi (רבי) and was taught from that time in Rabbi's study hall. And this view appears correct from that statement in Tractate Hagigah regarding those deaf-mutes who were in Rabbi's neighborhood, the sons of the sister of Rabbi Yohanan ben Gudgada (רבי יוחנן בן גודגדא). And the sons of the daughter of Rabbi Yohanan ben Gudgada said that whenever Rabbi would enter the study hall, they would enter and sit before him, moving their lips and nodding their heads. Rabbi prayed for them and they were healed, and it was found that they knew Halacha, Sifra, Sifrei, Tosefta, and the entire Talmud.

And what you asked: "What did Rabbi Hiyya (רבי חייא) see fit to write it, and why did Rabbi (רבי) not write it?" If Rabbi had wanted to write and compile everything that was taught in his days, the words would have been too lengthy and would have been forgotten. Rather, our Holy Rabbi established and wrote the core matters, such as general rules and concise language, so that even from a single matter one could learn many reasons and mounds upon mounds of great and wondrous halachot, for our Mishnah was stated with Heavenly assistance. And Rabbi Hiyya came and expanded in the Baraita the specifics and aspects that had roots and general rules. And most of the reasons that are expanded and elaborated upon in the Baraita have their roots in our Mishnah and rely upon the roots of our Mishnah, as we say: Ilfa (אילפא) hung himself from the mast of a ship and said, "If there is anyone who can ask me a matter from the school of Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Oshaya (רבי אושעיא) and I cannot resolve it from our Mishnah, I will fall from the mast and drown."

Thus, everything that is in Rabbi Hiyya (רבי חייא) and Rabbi Oshaya (רבי אושעיא) we can resolve from our Mishnah. And Ilfa (אילפא) came to show his wisdom because of that incident he had with Rabbi Yohanan (רבי יוחנן), and when that elder came and taught him, "He says, 'Give a shekel to my sons,' and they are fitting to be given a sela..." etc. "Whose view is this?" He established it according to Rabbi Meir (רבי מאיר) who said, "It is a mitzvah to fulfill the words of the dead." And if Rabbi Hiyya came in a Baraita to disagree with Rabbi (רבי), we do not listen to him, such as a matter that Rabbi saw as halacha and recorded anonymously in our Mishnah, even though there was a dispute about it originally. And just as Rabbi Hiyya explains that there was a dispute originally, even though it is anonymous in our Mishnah, we act according to our Mishnah. We do not follow the general rule we have regarding the disputes of the Sages, that between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yose (רבי יוסי), the halacha follows Rabbi Yose; rather, where Rabbi recorded an anonymous ruling like Rabbi Meir in our Mishnah, we act according to the anonymous ruling.

But where Rabbi (רבי) explicitly stated the dispute in our Mishnah, we act according to the general rule, for example: Rabbi Meir (רבי מאיר) says this and Rabbi Yose (רבי יוסי) says this, the halacha follows Rabbi Yose. And if Rabbi Hiyya (רבי חייא) saw the reasoning of Rabbi Meir who disputed with Rabbi Yose in our Mishnah, and recorded it anonymously in the Baraita like Rabbi Meir, we do not accept it from him. As Nahum (נחום), the servant of Rabbi Abbahu (רבי אבהו), asked Rabbi Abbahu: "An anonymous ruling in our Mishnah and a dispute in the Baraita—what is the rule?" He said to him: "The halacha follows the anonymous ruling of our Mishnah." "Because of a dispute in our Mishnah and an anonymous ruling in the Baraita—what is the rule?" He said to him: "If Rabbi did not teach it, from where did Rabbi Hiyya get it?" Because Rabbi Hiyya was the student of Rabbi. And what he taught him is what he said, and Rabbi Hiyya only had what Rabbi had, and even the exact wording of our Mishnah decides explicitly against the Baraita. Like that dispute regarding "A breach is like a standing wall," we say, "It is a conclusive refutation of Rav Pappa (רב פפא), a conclusive refutation, but the halacha follows Rav Pappa." And we ask, "A conclusive refutation and the halacha follows him?" And we answer, "Yes, because the exact deduction of our Mishnah follows his teaching, for it teaches 'provided the breaches are not greater than the standing structure.'"

And Sifra and Sifrei are expositions of the verses, showing where the halachot are hinted at in the verses. Originally, in the Second Temple period in the days of the early Sages, they taught them in this manner. And when the Sages saw that there were other Baraitot that were not from Rabbi Hiyya (רבי חייא) and Rabbi Oshaya (רבי אושעיא) that contained errors, specifics that looked like individual general rules, and matters that were not exact, they recognized that these Baraitot arranged by Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Oshaya were superior to all of them. The Sages collected them and taught them in the Yeshiva, and regarding them we say in the Gemara "Tanu Rabanan" (Our Rabbis taught). Nevertheless, other Baraitot were common, and each of the Sages studied what his master taught him. And the Tannaim also recited them before them, such as Ahi (אחי) the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Hiyya, and Ashiyan (אשייאן) the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Ammi (רבי אמי). Bar Kappara (בר קפרא) also taught other Mishnayot, and in several places we say, "As Levi (לוי) taught in his Mishnah," and "Levi decided it in his Mishnah." But those of Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Oshaya were superior to all of them. And each and every one of them had a Baraita of their own on each and every tractate, as we say: "Rav Sharvya (רב שרביא) taught in Kiddushin from the school of Levi." And he was also the student of Rabbi (רבי), like Bar Kappara, Rabbi Hiyya, and Rabbi Oshaya.

And the Sages of Babylon who were before our Holy Rabbi (רבי) also had Mishnayot, for there was much Torah among them, and they disseminated it in the place of the Yeshiva. As we learned: "Rabbi Akiva (רבי עקיבא) said, 'When I went down to Nehardea (נהרדעא) to intercalate the year...'" etc. And in Pumbedita (פומבדיתא), where Rabbi Hanina, nephew of Rabbi Yehoshua (רבי חנינא בן אחי רבי יהושע), was. And our Rabbis taught: "Follow a good court," and we explain: "After Rabbi Hanina, nephew of Rabbi Yehoshua, to the Golah (Diaspora)." And they called it Golah because they used to light beacons of the court there, as we learned: "Until he sees the entire Golah before him like a bonfire." And we say about this: "What is Golah? Abaye (אביי) said: Pumbedita."

And Hillel the Elder (הלל הזקן) came up from Babylon and was Nasi in the Land of Israel. And in the days of Rabbi (רבי) and after him, those Babylonian Mishnayot were called in the Land of Israel "The Mishnah of Rabbi Natan (רבי נתן)." And regarding Mar Shmuel (מר שמואל), we also say in several places, "The Tanna of the school of Shmuel." And those Mishnayot that the early Torah scholars taught were not stated in the name of Rabbi Akiva (רבי עקיבא), as we say in several places, "The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael (רבי ישמעאל)" and "The Tanna of the school of Eliezer ben Yaakov (אליעזר בן יעקב)." And there were also Baraitot of the earliest Sages, as we say in Tractate Eruvin: "Rabbah bar Mari (רבה בר מרי) taught from the school of Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai (רבן יוחנן בן זכאי)." And all these Baraitot were not fixed for everyone to study as the Baraitot of Rabbi Hiyya (רבי חייא) and Rabbi Oshaya (רבי אושעיא) were fixed, and we do not say about them "Tanu Rabanan," but rather "Tanya" and "Tana Tuna."

And Sifra and Sifrei were also not spread by the Rabbis initially like our Mishnah, which spread throughout the entire Land of Israel from the moment it was established; rather, they spread little by little. As we say: "I saw Ben Pedat (בן פדת) sitting and expounding like Moses," Rabbi Yohanan (רבי יוחנן) said to Resh Lakish (ריש לקיש), "from the mouth of the Almighty." Resh Lakish said to him, "It is not his, it is a Baraita! And where did he learn it? In Torat Kohanim." Rabbi Yohanan went out and taught it in three days and reasoned it in three months.

And after that, Sifra, Sifrei, and Tosefta were established, and all the Sages studied them, and until now this is the established practice. As Rav Nahman (רב נחמן) said there, "Behold, I and Rav Sheshet (רב ששת), who have studied the halachot, Sifra, Sifrei"—which all the Sages studied—"and Tosefta and the entire Talmud." And these Baraitot have no end or limit, and each and every one of the Sages studied them from the mouth of his master, as we say: Rav Pappa bar Abba (רב פפא בר אבא) found Rabbah bar Shaul (רבה בר שאול). He said to him, "Has the Master taught anything regarding a hired worker?" He said to him, "I have taught..."

And the Amoraic Sages (אמוראים) who came after Rabbi (רבי) heavily needed these Baraitot, for from them emerged all the deep matters that were stated in our Mishnah in concise language, in hints, and in general rules, and branches, novelties, and derivatives emerged from them. For Rabbi only arranged their roots and did not elaborate on their comparisons, and the Sages also needed dialectics (pilpul) and reasoning (sevara). And there were also among them those who needed a matter and needed to compare a matter to everything similar to it, bringing it back to its root. As we say: When Rav Hisda (רב חסדא) and Rav Sheshet (רב ששת) would meet each other, Rav Hisda would tremble from the Mishnayot of Rav Sheshet, and Rav Sheshet would tremble from the dialectics of Rav Hisda.

And the Sages praised the one who studied much Mishnah, as the reasons of the Torah were revealed to him, for since he learned and knew many teachings, he would teach a matter that one Master summarized and another Master expanded, and a matter that was deep in one Mishnah was clear in another Mishnah. As Rabbi Aha b'Rabbi Hanina (רבי אחא בר חנינא) said in the name of Rabbi Ammi (רבי אמי) in the name of Rabbi Assi (רבי אסי) in the name of Rabbi Yohanan (רבי יוחנן): "What is the meaning of the verse, 'For by wise guidance you shall make your war'? In whom do you find the war of Torah? In one who has in his hand bundles upon bundles of Mishnah." Rav Yosef (רב יוסף) applied to himself: "And abundant crops come by the strength of the ox."

And even though someone who learns but does not know how to engage in dialectics—which novelty and derivative comes from it that is not explicitly taught in our Mishnah—and does not know how to compare or extract its core from our Mishnah, nevertheless he is better than someone who engages in dialectics and reasons but has not learned what is taught or what was said. What is the reason? Because the one who has learned can teach those matters he heard as practical halacha, while the one who only reasons cannot. What is the reason? Because for the one who lacks learning, what do we derive for him from reasoning? But the one who has learning, it is according to what was said, and we do not derive it for him from learning alone.

And where the Amoraim (אמוראים) disagree, and the general course follows one of them, and a Baraita is taught like the other, we act according to the one whose teaching aligns with the Baraita. As we say in Shechitat Kodashim: Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehudah (רב יצחק בריה דרב יהודה) was frequently before Rami bar Hama (רמי בר חמא). He left him and went before Rav Sheshet (רב ששת). One day he met him. Rami bar Hama said to him, "The dignitary has taken us by the hand; the scent has come to his hand." He said to him, "Because you went before Rav Sheshet, you became like Rav Sheshet?" He said to him, "Not because of that, but when I need a matter from the Master, he resolves it for me from reasoning, and if I find a Baraita that refutes him, you say to me, 'If it is taught, it is taught.' But Rav Sheshet, when I need a matter from him, resolves it for me from a Baraita, and if I find a Baraita that refutes it, he says to me, 'It is one Baraita against another Baraita.'" He said to him, "Ask a matter of me, and it will be resolved for you from the reasoning of a Baraita." He asked him: "If part of a vessel was boiled in it, does the whole vessel require purging and rinsing, or does it not?" He said to him, "It does not require it." "What is the reason?" "Just as it is with sprinkling." He said to him, "But a Baraita does not teach this, for it is taught: If part of a vessel was boiled in it, the whole vessel requires purging and rinsing, which is not the case with sprinkling." He said to him, "If it is taught, it is taught."

And because of this, when they asked, "Sinai (סיני) and an Uprooter of Mountains (עוקר הרים)—which of them is better?" When the world needed Rabbah (רבה), who was an Uprooter of Mountains, and Rav Yosef (רב יוסף), who was a Sinai—as we say that he applied to himself, "And abundant crops come by the strength of the ox"—they sent from there: "Sinai is better, for everyone needs the master of wheat (which is learning)." This is how Rabbi Hiyya (רבי חייא) saw it and arranged his Baraitot, which are the ones now taught exclusively in the Yeshiva, because all those early ones had too much to learn and recite, and what the Rabbis needed from them, we say in the Gemara, analyzing them and extracting their reasons, and the rest were found to be unnecessary for us.

And even though the Baraitot of Rav (רב) and Shmuel (שמואל) in Babylon were exact and correct, as we say in the order of Yoma regarding the bull and goat whose blood is applied outside: Rava (רבא) said, "You only find it correct either according to Rabbi Eliezer (רבי אליעזר) of the school of Shmuel or Rabbi Akiva (רבי עקיבא) of the Tosefta," nevertheless, the one of the school of Shmuel was left aside. And when we find texts of Baraitot now, we do not rely upon them, for they are not taught, and we do not know if they are truthful or not, except those of Rabbi Hiyya (רבי חייא) alone, which were studied in the Yeshiva. And there are also other Baraitot which the Rabbis called 'truncated,' from which one does not issue rulings, such as Hilchot Derech Eretz (הלכות דרך ארץ) and other Aggadot (הגדות).

And regarding the Talmud (תלמוד) you asked about: Even the very first generations had a Talmud, for we say they had halachot that they studied, as we say, "An incident occurred where Ben Zakkai (בן זכאי) examined the stalks of figs." And even though they did not all recite it with one mouth and one language, the reasons are known to be the same, and they are all one. Each one taught his students compilations that differed from one another, each as his master had taught him. Their halachot and reasons were identical, even though their versions varied from one another.

And their principles were *Kal V'Homer* (a fortiori inferences), *Gezerot Shavot* (verbal analogies), and various methods of exegesis. Among them were the thirteen rules by which Rabbi Yishmael (רבי ישמעאל) expounded. And among them were other methods, such as rearranging verses, inclusions and exclusions, meanings of expressions, juxtaposition, comparison, two verses coming as one do not teach, learning the upper from the lower, "if you grasp a little you grasp it, if you grasp much you do not grasp it," seeking the reason of the verse, subtracting, adding, and expounding, "there is a mother for reading and a mother for tradition," stated here and stated there, a verse is expounded before it and before its face, a verse does not depart from its plain meaning, there is no early and late in the Torah, the Torah speaks in the language of men, hints, a matter stated regarding one thing that is irrelevant to it, apply it to its fellow, a matter whose fellow proves its meaning, a matter stated in this and that and is irrelevant, apply it to its fellow, a section stated and repeated was only repeated for the novelty in it, derive from it and from it, derive from it and establish it in its place, it is sufficient for the derived to be like the source. And many things like these. When those early ones stated their halachot, each one as he learned them, these matters constituted their Talmud to reveal the reasons of the Torah. As Rabbi Abbahu (רבי אבהו) said in the name of Rabbi Yohanan (רבי יוחנן): "Rabbi Meir (רבי מאיר) had one student, and his name was Symmachus (סומכוס), who would state forty-eight reasons of impurity for every matter of impurity, and forty-eight reasons of purity for every matter of purity."
And similarly, they had another aspect to their Talmud: to see novelties, branches, and derivatives—what their laws were, what their comparisons were, and how we return the branch to its root.

And how do we know they had a Talmud? For regarding Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai (רבן יוחנן בן זכאי) they said that he had mastered even the debates of Abaye (אביי) and Rava (רבא). And we also learned: Rabbi Yehudah (רבי יהודה) says, "Be careful in Talmud, for an inadvertent error in Talmud amounts to a deliberate sin." And our Rabbis taught: "He who engages in Scripture—it is a measure that is not a measure. In Mishnah—it is a measure for which they receive reward. In Talmud—you have no measure greater than this."

And after Rabbi (רבי) established the halacha and our Mishnah, they had a Talmud in which they explained the exactitude of our Mishnah, the specifics, the general rules, and the reasons of the exegeses. As our Rabbis taught: "Run to the Mishnah more than to the Talmud." And we say concerning this: "This itself is contradictory! You said, 'In Talmud—you have no measure greater than this,' and then you said, 'Run to the Mishnah more than to the Talmud'?" Rabbi Yohanan (רבי יוחנן) said: "In the days of Rabbi this Mishnah was taught: 'In Talmud—you have no measure greater than this.' Everyone abandoned the Mishnayot and went after the Talmud. He then expounded for them: 'Always run to the Mishnah more than to the Talmud.'" What did he expound? As Rabbi Yehudah b'Rabbi Ilai (רבי יהודה ברבי אילעאי) expounded: "Declare to My people their transgression, and to the house of Jacob their sins. 'Declare to My people their transgression'—these are Torah scholars whose inadvertent errors become like deliberate sins. 'And to the house of Jacob their sins'—these are the ignorant, for whom even deliberate sins become like inadvertent errors." And this is what we learned: Rabbi Yehudah says, "Be careful in Talmud, for an inadvertent error in Talmud amounts to a deliberate sin."

And the Talmud is the wisdom of the early ones who deduced the reasons of the Mishnah, as our Rabbis taught: "His master who they said—not his master who taught him Scripture, and not his master who taught him Mishnah, but his master who taught him Talmud." There are those who teach, "His master who taught him wisdom," and both are the same reason. For that which teaches "his master, not his master who taught him Scripture, and not his master who taught him Mishnah, but his master who taught him Talmud," these are the words of Rabbi Meir (רבי מאיר). Rabbi Yehudah (רבי יהודה) says, "Anyone from whom the majority of his wisdom comes." Rabbi Yose (רבי יוסי) says, "Even if he only illuminated his eyes in one Mishnah, this is his master." And Rava (רבא) said, "Like Rav Sehora (רב סחורא) who explained 'zoma listran' to me."

And before Rabbi (רבי) passed away, they did not have a written composition that they learned by heart, but rather they wrote commentaries for it, which we (and those like us) now explain to our students who all learn it. And this one wrote in one way, and that one wrote in another way, as they saw fit; thus they explained their Mishnayot and called their commentaries 'Talmud.' The heart was broad, and they only needed the roots. But when the Mishnah was completed and Rabbi passed away, the heart diminished, and they needed to collect their Talmud and learn it by heart. They added many other ways to it, and those earliest Sages established within it, as we say, "From where do we derive these matters? We expound verses." And they established within it novelties and derivatives, matter by matter, as it is explained, just as it was in the days of the ancients. And they also established in it what the early ones did not need, such as the explanation of deep matters that the early ones, whose hearts were broad, did not need to explain, and wisdom diminished after them. As our Rabbis taught: "From the time Rabbi Eliezer (רבי אליעזר) died, the Torah scroll was hidden. From the time Rabbi Yehoshua (רבי יהושע) died, counsel, humility, and thought ceased. And from the time Rabbi Akiva (רבי עקיבא) died, the arms of Torah ceased and the wellsprings of wisdom were sealed." And this also happened in the days of Rabbi.

And they established other deductions in it, matter after matter: Why was this taught? And they say, "Let's see, he taught this, why did he need to teach that as well?" And where they could not resolve it, we say, "Here Rabbi (רבי) taught an unnecessary Mishnah," and we derive the necessity of each and every matter, asking, "What does this come to teach us?" And they detail the specifics and compare the comparisons. All these matters, as they were in the days of Rabbi, he would explain the commentary of every matter and its practical halachic outcome. And they needed other things that the early ones did not need, such as where Rabbi saw a matter but the later Sages did not see it, they explained it so as not to rely on it. For example, where Rabbi anonymously recorded the words of an individual because the halacha seemed to follow him, but it did not seem so to the later Sages. Like the matter of the mitzvah of Halitzah, because when an individual said something and Rabbi saw that his reason was halacha, he taught it anonymously. As we say regarding the widow in Ketubot: "Whose view is this? It is Rabbi Shimon (רבי שמעון)." And regarding one who died, concerning acquisition by a terminally ill person on Shabbat: "Our Mishnah is Rabbi Yehudah (רבי יהודה)." And in "He brought him the spoon," they also eagerly give a sign. And many like these, where it tells you, "Whose view is this? It is Rabbi so-and-so," and it was taught by an individual, even though Rabbi left it anonymous, we do not follow it.

And where he left it anonymous in a place of dispute, it is even stronger. Like that which we learned: "Halitzah and refusals are before three," which is explained in the mitzvah of Halitzah. Alternatively, he taught the statement of an individual in the language of the Sages so that they would act according to it. As Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba (רבי חייא בר אבא) said in the name of Rabbi Yohanan (רבי יוחנן): "Rabbi saw the words of Rabbi Meir (רבי מאיר) in 'It and its offspring' and taught them in the language of the Sages, and he saw the words of Rabbi Shimon (רבי שמעון) in 'Covering the blood' and taught them in the language of the Sages."

And from here we also learn that an anonymous statement of Rabbi Meir (רבי מאיר) is not his own individual opinion, but rather that of his masters, from his master Rabbi Akiva (רבי עקיבא). Therefore, when Rabbi (רבי) knew that this statement of Rabbi Meir in 'It and its offspring' was from his masters, he taught it in the language of the Sages. And just as we learned regarding leaven that is to be burned, "The Sages say: One who eats this or that is liable to excision (Karet)," and he did not teach it in the name of Rabbi Meir, who disagrees with Rabbi Yehudah (רבי יהודה), so that people would not err and say that our general rule is that between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah, the halacha follows Rabbi Yehudah; rather, the halacha follows Rabbi Meir. As Rava (רבא) said: "What is the reason of Rabbi Meir? There is not a single crack from above..." etc., and it is also taught thus in a Baraita.

Now, the Amoraic Sages (אמוראים) of the Talmud come and explain these matters. Where they saw as Rabbi (רבי) saw, the matter is revealed to them that the halacha follows that individual. And where they did not see as Rabbi saw, and the matter was not revealed to them—like in "He who brings" in Tractate Yom Tov: Rabbi Yehudah (רבי יהודה) said in the name of Shmuel (שמואל), "One may only bring wood from what is gathered in the enclosure." And we object: "But didn't we learn: 'From the enclosure, and even from the scattered'?" This is a conclusive refutation of Shmuel! And we answer: "The Mishnah is the view of an individual, and it also found support from a Baraita."

And where we find a corrupted matter in our Mishnah, and we need to remove something from it because it poses an unanswerable difficulty, we say, "Remove such and such from it." Like those of 'It and its offspring,' where we say: Rabbi Hiyya (רבי חייא) said in the name of Rabbi Yohanan (רבי יוחנן), "The Red Heifer is not a Mishnah, the Broken-Necked Heifer is not a Mishnah." Thus, if a Mishnah is difficult and cannot be resolved from a Baraita, and even from logical reasoning, we reject the entire Mishnah. Like the one we learned in Taharot: "A flax comb whose teeth were removed." And we say in HaHoleitz: "Rabbi Yohanan and Resh Lakish (ריש לקיש) both say, 'This is not a Mishnah, and we do not act according to it,' because of those who strictly mark the ends..." etc.

And if a Mishnah needs text added, we add to it, and if it needs to be corrected, we correct it. And if there is an error in the Mishnah, and a Baraita is superior to it, we clarify the matter from it. As we learned: "The House of Shammai say: An Israelite may not be counted with a Kohen for a firstborn animal, and the House of Hillel permit, and even a non-Jew." And we say on this in the Gemara: "The House of Hillel of our Mishnah is Rabbi Akiva (רבי עקיבא) of the Baraita. The halacha follows Rabbi Akiva of the Baraita, who said: Even non-Kohanim, but not non-Jews."

And if the Tannaim (תנאים) disagree, we say, "In what do they disagree?" And we state the reason for each and every one of them, and we search for a common Baraita to clarify the matter, or to resolve that question from them, and we state them from wherever we find them. Like that of "He who dispatches" in Tractate Gittin, where Rabbi Yirmeyah (רבי ירמיה) said to Rabbi Zerika (רבי זריקא): "Go out and examine it in your collection."

And we scrutinize them meticulously, and we conclude each one according to its reason and its halacha, and each one—who said it, and according to whom they are, apart from the disputes of the Amoraim. And their difficulties, answers, refutations, resolutions, rejections, establishments, puzzlements, and wonders, and to expand and write the paths of the Talmud, which are very numerous.

And this is how it was in the time of the early Sages, just as we now explain our commentaries. Each and every one of the great masters taught each of his students according to what they needed and what they were capable of receiving. Some were given chapter headings and core principles, and the rest they understood from their own minds. And some needed them to expand, broaden, and compare comparisons for them.

And we say that until Rabbi (רבי) passed away, the learning of all the students was each individual student before his master, and before the Mishnah was established, each one's Talmud was according to his own Mishnah. And after it was established, all the days of Rabbi, he explained our Mishnah to everyone and taught them the reasons for his halachot. And after Rabbi passed away, they needed to collect it and recite it with one mouth and one language.

And after Rabbi (רבי), there were Tannaim from there, such as Rabbi Natan (רבי נתן) and Rabbi Shimon (רבי שמעון) and Rabbi Gamliel (רבי גמליאל) his sons. And from here, such as Rabbi Yoshiyah (רבי יאשיה) of Hutzal. However, they did not teach anything from the Mishnah other than what the Tannaim taught before this, as explained in the book of the First Man: "Rabbi and Rabbi Natan are the end of the Mishnah." And there were also other Sages who were both Tannaim and Amoraim, such as Rabbi Hanina (רבי חנינא) and Rabbi Yannai (רבי ינאי) there, and Rav (רב) here, who were the students of Rabbi and learned from Rabbi and Rabbi Hiyya (רבי חייא). As we say: Rabbi Yohanan (רבי יוחנן) said, "I remember when we were sitting seventeen rows behind Rav, and Rav was before Rabbi, and sparks of fire were flying from the mouth of Rabbi to the mouth of Rav, and from the mouth of Rav to the mouth of Rabbi, and I did not know what they were saying." And in several places we say: "Rav is a Tanna and can disagree."

And there were also other Sages who were solely Amoraim (אמוראים), such as Shmuel (שמואל) and Rabbi Shila (רבי שילא) and Rabbah bar bar Hana (רבה בר בר חנה) and Rav Kahana (רב כהנא) the first and Rav Assi (רב אסי). And in their days, at their end, were Rav Adda bar Ahavah (רב אדא בר אהבה) and Rabbah bar Avuha (רבה בר אבוה) our ancestor, and he is from the House of the Nasi. It is from the Sages that we hold by tradition that we are from the House of the Nasi and from the seed of Rabbah bar Avuha.

And after this was Rabbi Hanina (רבי חנינא) there, and Rabbi Yannai (רבי ינאי), Rabbi Yohanan (רבי יוחנן), Resh Lakish (ריש לקיש), Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi (רבי יהושע בן לוי), and Rabbi Elazar (רבי אלעזר), whose teachings were heard, and the teachings of Rav (רב) and Shmuel (שמואל) in Babylon. And even so, the wisdom in Babylon was much greater. And after their generation came Rav Nahman (רב נחמן), Rav Yehudah (רב יהודה), Rav Huna (רב הונא), Rav Hisda (רב חסדא), and Rav Sheshet (רב ששת) in Babylon, and other Sages who went up and came down, such as Ulla (עולא), Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba (רבי חייא בר אבא), and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani (רבי שמואל בר נחמני). And the Sages from there who came up from here were Rabbi Ammi (רבי אמי) and Rabbi Assi (רבי אסי). And after this, Rabbah (רבה) and Rav Yosef (רב יוסף) in Babylon. And the Sages who went up and came down, such as Rabbi Abba (רבי אבא)—who was greater than those early ones—and Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha (רבי יצחק נפחא), Rabbi Zeira (רבי זירא), Rabbi Yirmeyah (רבי ירמיה), Rabbi Abbahu (רבי אבהו), and Rabbi Hanina bar Papi (רבי חנינא בר פפי). And after this, Abaye (אביי) and Rava (רבא). And persecution increased in the Land of Israel, and instruction diminished there greatly, and those Babylonians who were there came down, such as Ravin (רבין) and Rav Dimi (רב דימי), and all the 'descenders' who came down here.

And in every single generation of these generations, they had teachings that the Sages recited and constantly reviewed. As we say: Rabbi Hiyya son of Rav Abba (רבי חייא בריה דרב אבא) used to review his Talmud before Rabbi Yohanan (רבי יוחנן) every thirty days. And we also say: Rav Sheshet (רב ששת) reviewed his Talmud every thirty days. He would lean on the bolt of the door and say, "Rejoice, my soul! Rejoice, my soul! For you I have read Scripture, for you I have studied Mishnah." And these teachings that everyone recited, every great master explained to his students with other explanations and extra precision. They also innovated, drawing practical conclusions from questions they were asked, and they debated among themselves, each one except his partner.

And another generation came, and hearts diminished. Those matters that were simple to the early ones, and which they explained to their students—being the kind of explanations that not everyone needed to study and fix in the Gemara—were now, in this generation, subject to doubt. They needed to fix them in the Gemara and in recitation, and they stated them in the Yeshiva, fixed them in the Gemara, and all the Sages recited them. As we say regarding an Eruv placed in a tree: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba (רבי חייא בר אבא), Rabbi Assi (רבי אסי), and Rabbah bar Natan (רבה בר נתן) were sitting, and Rav Nahman (רב נחמן) sat with them. They sat and were saying, "This tree that stands, where is it? If we say it stands in a private domain..." etc. And we say at the end: Rav Nahman said to them, "Excellent! And so said Shmuel (שמואל)." They said to him, "Did you interpret it this much as well?" He said to them, "You too interpreted it this much! What I mean to tell you is that you have also fixed it in the Gemara."

And every successive generation's heart diminishes. As we say: Rabbi Yohanan (רבי יוחנן) said, "Our heart is like the eye of a fine needle." And Abaye (אביי) said, "And we are like a peg in a wall for the Gemara." And Rava (רבא) said, "And we are like a finger in wax for reasoning." And Rav Ashi (רב אשי) said, "And we are like a finger in a pit for forgetting." And as much as the heart diminished and doubts arose, those explanations of the early ones that were not fixed in their days were fixed now and recited, and the practical rulings of those early Sages were now taught in the Gemara.

And if all the Sages heard a matter and said it as one, and no one preceded in hearing and saying it, it is stated anonymously, such as "so-and-so said." And if one preceded in hearing and saying it, it is stated in his name, "Rabbi so-and-so said." As we say: Ulla (עולא) visited Pumbedita. Rav Yehudah (רב יהודה) said to Rav Yitzhak (רב יצחק) his son, "Go bring him a basket of fruit, and see how he makes Havdalah." He went and sent Abaye (אביי). When he returned, he said to him, "He said 'He who distinguishes between holy and profane.'" He came and said to his father, "I did not go, I sent Abaye, and he told me he said 'He who distinguishes between holy and profane.'" He said, "The master's arrogance and haughtiness caused it that the halacha will not be stated in his name."

And the more exact a Sage is, and states a teaching from the mouth of a great master rather than from others, his teaching is superior. As we say: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak (רב נחמן בר יצחק) said, "Ulla (עולא) fixed his error like Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet (רבי בנימין בר יפת); let Rabbi Zeira (רבי זירא) wonder at it." And what does Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet have to do with Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba (רבי חייא בר אבא)? Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba was exact and learned teachings from the mouth of his master, while Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet was not exact. Furthermore, when he states it from the mouth of one great master, it is much superior. As we say: When Rabbi Zeira went up, he ate an improperly slaughtered animal of Rav (רב) and Shmuel (שמואל). They said to him, "Are you not from the place of Rav and Shmuel?" He said to them, "Who said it? Yosef bar Hiyya (יוסף בר חייא)." Yosef bar Hiyya learned from everyone. Rav Yosef heard this and became angry. He said, "Did I learn from everyone? I learned from Rav Yehudah (רב יהודה), for he recites even the doubts of great men. As Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rabbi Yirmeyah bar Abba (רבי ירמיה בר אבא)—doubtful in the name of Rav, doubtful in the name of Shmuel—three may permit a firstborn animal in a place where there is no expert."

And where all the Sages say one matter, they say it accordingly in these matters at the end of the Talmud, generation after generation. For in every generation they fix in the Talmud matters from the doubts that were renewed for them, and incidents and questions that were asked of them. Like that in Tractate Sanhedrin, where we say: Rav Kahana (רב כהנא) and Rav Safra (רב ספרא) were studying Sanhedrin in the school of Rabbah (רבה). Rami bar Hama (רמי בר חמא) met them and said to them, "And what do you say in the Sanhedrin of the school of Rabbah?" They said to him, "And what do we say in Sanhedrin itself, and the entire teaching!"

And the later Sages added and innovated precise deductions and arguments. It is not that the early Sages did not know them, but rather they left them for the generation that came after them to distinguish themselves with them, and the world did not need them in their days. As our Rabbis taught: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Zariz (רבי יהושע בן זריז), the father-in-law of Rabbi Meir (רבי מאיר), testified before Rabbi (רבי) concerning Rabbi Meir that he ate a leaf of a vegetable in Beit She'an, and Rabbi permitted all of Beit She'an based on him. His brothers and his father's house joined against him and said to him, "A place where your fathers and your fathers' fathers practiced a prohibition, you practice a permission?" He expounded this verse for them: "'And he broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made, for until those days the children of Israel burned incense to it, and he called it Nehushtan.' Is it possible that Asa came and did not destroy it, Jehoshaphat came and did not destroy it, but did not Asa and Jehoshaphat destroy all the idolatry in the world? Rather, his ancestors left room for him to distinguish himself; for me as well, my ancestors left me room to distinguish myself." From here we learn regarding a Torah scholar who states a matter of halacha, we do not neglect him (maznihin), and some say we do not move him (mazihin), and some say we do not make him arrogant (mazhihin). He who says 'we do not neglect him'—as it is written, "For the Lord will not cast off (yiznah) forever." And he who says 'we do not move him'—as it is written, "And the breastplate shall not be loosed (yizach)." And he who says 'we do not make him arrogant'—as we learned, "When those of arrogant hearts (zehuhei) multiplied, disputes multiplied in Israel."

And this is the answer to what you asked: "What is the reason the early ones left the majority for the later ones?" For if you find a wondrous thing that the later ones said, the early ones left it for them to distinguish themselves with it, and also to expand on these matters that were added to the Talmud generation after generation, of which there are many. As we say: Rabbi Ammi (רבי אמי) said, "Doeg and Ahithophel raised four hundred questions concerning a tower floating in the air." And Rava (רבא) said, "Is it greatness to raise questions? For in the years of Rav Yehudah (רב יהודה), all their study in Nezikin was 'A woman who preserves a vegetable in a pot,' and they would say to him, 'Olives that were preserved in their leaves are pure.' He would say, 'I see here the arguments of Rav (רב) and Shmuel (שמואל).' Yet we study thirteen tractates. And when Rav Yehudah took off his shoe, rain would come, whereas we afflict ourselves and no one pays attention to us. But the Holy One, Blessed be He, desires the heart."

And according to this, instruction was added generation after generation until Ravina (רבינא), and after Ravina it ceased, as Shmuel Yarchina'ah (שמואל ירחינאה) saw in the book of the First Man, where it was written: "Rav Ashi (רב אשי) and Ravina are the end of instruction." And after this, even though instruction certainly ceased, there were Saboraim (סבוראים) who explained commentaries that approach instruction. And these great masters were called Rabbanan Saborai (רבנן סבוראי), and they explained everything that was left pending. Such as Rav Rihumi (רב ריחומי), Rabbah (רבה), Rav Yosef (רב יוסף), and Rav Aha of Bei Hatim (רב אחא מבי חתים), as we say in HaMevi Get: "Also from Medinat HaYam and Ziklag..." etc., and Bei Hatim is a city in the vicinity of Nehardea. And Rav Rabbai of Rov (רב רבאי מרוב), as explained in Tractate Sanhedrin: Rabbi said, "One going out to be executed, they give him to drink a grain of frankincense in a cup of wine so his mind will be confused, as it is stated: 'Give strong drink to him who is perishing, and wine to those in bitter distress.'" And it was taught: "Noble women of Jerusalem would volunteer and bring it from their own." And we ask: "And if they do not volunteer it, from whose property does it come?" Rav Rabbai of Rov taught: "It makes sense that it comes from the public funds, because it says 'Give.'" And Rov, the city of Rav Rabbai, was also in the vicinity of the Yeshivot of Nehardea. And the Sages say that Rav Rabbai was a Gaon and lived many years. And many Saboraic additions were fixed in the Gemara, for they are from the later Sages, such as Rav Eina (רב עינא) and Rav Simuna (רב סימונא). We derive from the early parts of the Gemara of "A woman is acquired" [which we teach at the beginning: "From where do we derive these matters?..." etc.] up until "From where do we derive 'with money'?" All those difficulties and answers that the Gemara resolves, the later Saboraic Sages resolved them and fixed them.

And regarding what you wrote: "How was the Mishnah written, and how was the Talmud written?" The Talmud and Mishnah were not written; rather, their arrangements were arranged, and the Sages were careful to recite them by heart, but not from written texts. As we say: "Things stated orally, you are not permitted to state them in writing, as it is stated: 'For by the mouth of these words I have made a covenant with you...' These you may write, but you may not write halachot."

And regarding what you asked: "How were the Saboraic Rabbis (רבנן סבוראי) ordered after Ravina (רבינא), and who reigned after them from that time until now?" We see fit to explain to you the essence of this matter: how the authority of Israel was formerly, and how the two Yeshivot were divided, because there is an erroneous matter in it. Know that initially, when Israel was exiled in the exile of Jeconiah with the craftsmen and the smiths, and many prophets with them, they brought them to Nehardea (נהרדעא). Jeconiah, King of Judah, and his faction built a synagogue there, establishing it with stones and earth they brought with them from the Holy Temple to fulfill what is stated: "For Your servants take pleasure in her stones, and favor her dust." And they called that synagogue 'Shaf V'Yativ' (שף ויתיב) [which is in Nehardea], meaning that the Holy Temple traveled and settled here. And the Divine Presence was with them, as we say: "In Babylon, where does the Divine Presence dwell? Rav (רב) said: In the synagogue of Hutzal. And Shmuel (שמואל) said: In the synagogue of Shaf V'Yativ. And do not say here and not there, but rather say sometimes here and sometimes there. Abaye (אביי) said: May it come to me, for when I am a parasang away, I pray there." And this synagogue of Hutzal is close to the study hall of Ezra the Scribe and is below Nehardea.

And when Ezra, Zerubbabel, and the exiles went up from Babylon and built the Holy Temple, the heads of the Sanhedrin were there, such as Shimon HaTzaddik (שמעון הצדיק), Antigonus of Sokho (אנטיגנוס איש סוכו), and the rest of those 'Pairs' (Zugot), and most of them went up from Babylon. Hillel the Elder (הלל הזקן) went up with them, and nevertheless, they disseminated Torah here, and they had Exilarchs (Rashei Galuyot) from the House of David, but they did not have Heads of Yeshivot and Sanhedrin among them, for they say this matter is only from "the place that the Lord shall choose."

And until Rabbi (רבי) passed away, the Exilarch led in Babylon, and not the Heads of Yeshivot. And the Nesi'im, who are the heads of the Sanhedrin in the Land of Israel, as explained in Avot up to Hillel and Shammai. And after Hillel, Shimon (שמעון) his son. And after him, Rabban Gamliel the Elder (רבן גמליאל הזקן) his son. And after him, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel the First (רבן שמעון בן גמליאל), who was killed before the destruction of the Temple, and Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha (רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע) was the High Priest. And these four generations were included in those hundred years that we say in the Exits of Shabbat: "Hillel, Shimon, Gamliel, and Shimon conducted their presidency before the Temple for a hundred years."

And after Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel (רבן שמעון בן גמליאל) who was killed among the Martyrs of the Kingdom, there was Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai (רבן יוחנן בן זכאי), who was at the time of the destruction of the Temple. They brought him out to Vespasian (אספסינוס) Caesar, and he requested from him the dynasty of Rabban Gamliel, and Yavneh and its Sages. And when Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai and the Sages settled in Yavneh, they established ten enactments for them. As we learned: "When the Temple was destroyed, Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai enacted..." And after him was Rabban Gamliel, son of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel the Elder who was killed with the Ten Martyrs of the Kingdom. And that Rabban Gamliel his son was the Nasi in Yavneh, and Rabbi Yehoshua (רבי יהושע) was the Head of the Court. And since he pained Rabbi Yehoshua three times, they removed him and appointed Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah (רבי אלעזר בן עזריה), who was wealthy and tenth in descent to Ezra the Scribe. And then they appeased him and returned it to Rabban Gamliel, and they did not remove Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah, but Rabban Gamliel taught two Sabbaths and Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah one Sabbath, as explained in the Gemara of the Morning Prayer. And after him was Rabbi Shimon (רבי שמעון) his son, father of Rabbi, who was Nasi. And after him was Rabbi (רבי) his son, who was in Tzippori and Beit She'arim.

And in the days of Rabbi (רבי), Rav Huna the First (רב הונא) was the Exilarch in Babylon. And this is what we say: Rabbi asked Rabbi Hiyya (רבי חייא), "Someone like me, what am I regarding a male goat [offering for a Nasi]?" He said to him, "Behold, your rival is in Babylon [and who is it? Rav Huna]." And Rav Safra (רב ספרא) teaches that this is what he said to him: "There is the scepter, and here is the lawgiver." As it is taught: "'The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the lawgiver from between his feet.' 'The scepter shall not depart from Judah'—these are the Exilarchs in Babylon who subjugate the people with staffs. 'And the lawgiver from between his feet'—these are the descendants of Hillel who teach Torah in public." Thus, those in Babylon are superior, since they hold the scepter.

And in the days of Rabbi (רבי), Rav Huna (רב הונא) in Babylon passed away. And the Sages explain in the Talmud of the Land of Israel that Rabbi was extremely humble, and Rabbi used to say: "Whatever a person tells me to do, I will do, except for what the Elders of Bathyra did for Hillel the Elder, when they removed themselves from their presidency and appointed him. But if Rav Huna the Exilarch were to come up here, I would seat him above me, for he is from the tribe of Judah and I am from the tribe of Benjamin; he is from the male line of Judah, and I am from the female line." One time, Rabbi Hiyya the Great (רבי חייא רבה) entered before him and said, "Behold, Rav Huna is outside." Rabbi's face blanched. He said to him, "His coffin has arrived." Rabbi said to Rabbi Hiyya, "Go out and see who wants you outside." He went out and found no one, and Rabbi Hiyya knew that Rabbi was angry with him. He took upon himself a reprimand for thirty days and did not enter before Rabbi for thirty days. Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Bun (רבי יוסי ברבי בון) said: "In those thirty days, Rav learned from him all the general rules of the Torah."

And after Rav Huna (רב הונא) in Babylon, Mar Rav Ukva (מר רב עוקבא) was appointed. And Shmuel (שמואל) was with him, as we say: Shmuel and Mar Ukva, when they sat and learned, Mar Ukva would sit before Shmuel at his four cubits. And when they sat in judgment, Shmuel would sit before Mar Ukva at his four cubits. And we say: Shmuel said to Rav Yehudah (רב יהודה), "Sharp one! Your head is in cold water, and the head of your master is in hot water. Behold, Mar Ukva and his court exist, and it is written concerning them, 'Thus says the Lord, O house of David, execute justice in the morning.'"

And in the days of Rabbi (רבי), Rav (רב) went down to Babylon in the year 530 of the Greek era (Seleucid era), which we are accustomed to using. And Rabbi Shila (רבי שילא) was here as the head of the Sages after Rabbi, and he was called the 'Resh Sidra' (Head of the Order) in Babylon, the head of the Sages. As we say: Rav happened to visit the place of Rabbi Shila, and he stood up for him as an interpreter. And when Rabbi Shila passed away, Rav and Shmuel (שמואל) were here, and Rav deferred to Shmuel. Rav did not want to be head over him and seat Shmuel before him, and Shmuel also did not want to be head over Rav and seat Rav before him, for Rav was much older than Shmuel. Like that which we say in the Gemara of Merubah: Rav, Shmuel, and Rav Assi (רב אסי) happened to attend a 'Shavua HaBen' (circumcision feast), and some say a 'Yeshua HaBen' (redemption of the son). Rav would not enter before Shmuel, Shmuel would not enter before Rav Assi, and Rav Assi would not enter before Rav. They said, "Who should be troubled?" Shmuel was troubled [and entered first], and then Rav. Shmuel was different, because Rav deferred to him due to that incident where he cursed him.

And because of this, Rav (רב) left Shmuel (שמואל) in Nehardea (נהרדעא), which was his place and a place of Torah, and he distanced himself to a place where there was no Torah, which is Sura (סורא), that is, Mata Mehasya (מתא מחסיה). And there were many Israelites there, and they did not even know the laws of forbidden and permitted. And Rav said, "I will sit here so that there will be Torah in this place." Like that incident explained in 'Kol HaBasar': Rav found an open valley and built a fence around it, and when he visited Tatlefush, he taught them and instructed them regarding the prohibition of udder, and he was called 'Resh Sidra'. As Rabbi Yohanan (רבי יוחנן) said to Issi ben Hini (איסי בן היני): "Who is the Resh Sidra in Babylon?" He said to him: "Abba Arikha (אבא אריכא)." The dream that Rabbi Hanina (רבי חנינא) saw about him was fulfilled, that they hoisted him there, as explained in the chapter of Yom Kippur.

And Rav (רב) acquired the garden of the school of Rav in an area of desolation, which was the property of a proselyte, and he gathered many students there, disseminated much Torah, and established a court there. And there were two great courts in Babylon: one in Nehardea (נהרדעא) which already existed, and one in Sura (סורא) which Rav established. And this is what Shmuel (שמואל) said: "We only write a prozbul in the court of Sura or in the court of Nehardea." And Rav and Shmuel thus had two Yeshivot. As we say in "One who brings a Get from Medinat HaYam": "Babylon: Rav says it is like the Land of Israel for Gittin, and Shmuel says it is like the Diaspora." And we resolve it: "Since Rav holds that there are Yeshivot, one can find witnesses; and Shmuel holds that the Yeshivot are busy with their studies." And occasionally Rav and Shmuel would see one another.
